title: In John 20 In What Ways Does Thomas Doubt Resonate With Our Own Struggles In Faith And How Can We Find Assurance In Christs Response
paragraphs: The Doubt of Thomas: Our Struggles and Christ’s Assurance

Thomas, often remembered as “Doubting Thomas,” features prominently in John 20. His story is not just about skepticism; it is a profound reflection of the spiritual journey many believers experience. Let us explore the dynamics of Thomas’s doubt, how it mirrors our own struggles, and the hope we find in Christ’s compassionate response.
Thomas’s Doubt: Honest and Relatable
After Jesus’ resurrection, He appeared to His disciples. Yet Thomas was not present at first. When the others told him they had seen the Lord, Thomas demanded tangible proof:
Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe. - John 20:25 ASV

Thomas’s insistence on physical evidence resonates with our own desire for certainty, especially when faith is tested by hardship, unanswered prayers, or intellectual challenges. His honesty is striking—he voices his doubts rather than hiding them. The Bible does not condemn such questioning; rather, it presents Thomas as a real person grappling with belief.
Our Struggles with Doubt
Like Thomas, we sometimes wrestle with:
Intellectual Doubts: Questions about the reliability of Scripture or the reality of miracles.
Emotional Doubts: Seasons of suffering, loss, or disappointment that make God feel distant.
Spiritual Doubts: Feeling unworthy of God’s love or forgiveness, wondering if faith is “enough.”

Scripture acknowledges these struggles. Even John the Baptist, who had proclaimed Jesus as the Lamb of God, later questioned if Jesus was truly the Messiah (Matthew 11:2-3 ASV). The Psalms are filled with honest cries of confusion and longing (Psalm 13:1 ASV).
Christ’s Response: Grace, Invitation, and Assurance
What is remarkable is not just Thomas’s doubt, but how Jesus responds:
Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and see my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and put it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing. - John 20:27 ASV
Jesus meets Thomas where he is. He does not rebuke him harshly, but gently invites him to see and believe. Thomas’s honest confession follows:
Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God. - John 20:28 ASV
This is the highest confession of faith recorded in John’s Gospel. In response, Jesus gives a word for all future believers:
Jesus saith unto him, Because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed. - John 20:29 ASV
Finding Assurance Today
Thomas’s story teaches us several important lessons:
God Welcomes Honest Doubt: Sincere searching is not rejected by Christ. He honors those who seek Him (Jeremiah 29:13 ASV).
Assurance Is Found in Christ: Our faith is not based on feelings or perfect understanding, but on the risen Lord, who invites us to trust Him (Romans 10:17 ASV).
Blessed Are Those Who Believe: Jesus pronounces a special blessing on those who have not seen, yet believe—a category that includes all believers today.
The Word Is Sufficient: John’s Gospel emphasizes that the written testimony is given so readers may believe and have life (John 20:31 ASV).
Living Out Faith Amid Doubt

If you are struggling with doubts, bring them honestly to God in prayer. Seek answers in Scripture, and remember that faith is ultimately trust in the character and promises of Christ. Assurance is not the absence of questions, but the presence of Christ who answers, “Do not disbelieve, but believe.”
